title: How to Embed Writing Instruction Into Your English Curriculum
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that asking pupils to write extended essays before they have been taught and have practised each component tells teachers little, and often mistakes untaught fluency for ability. He explains how the C25K Writing programme, modelled on Couch to 5k, splits writing into nine Deconstructed Essay sentences and thirty creative sentences spread across Years 7 to 9. Two rules govern the sequence: no more than one new essay sentence and two new creative sentences per half term, and every practice task tied to curriculum content. He sketches a half term of weekly steps on The Odyssey, ending in a checkpoint every pupil is expected to pass. Three leadership moves matter most: change assessment first, delay extended writing in favour of short controlled bursts, and teach the controlling idea sentence out of order. Part of the piece describes his paid progression pack, but the sequencing logic stands on its own.
points: Extended-essay assessment mostly reveals who learned to write despite the teaching, so mastery checks on what has actually been taught are more informative.
The programme caps new content at one essay sentence and two creative sentences per half term, with earlier material kept alive through retrieval.
Changing KS3 assessment first matters because GCSE-style essay marking squeezes out sentence-level instruction.
If pupils fail a checkpoint, the diagnosis is insufficient practice or faulty instruction, not weak pupils.
quotes: In the overwhelming majority of schools, children are assessed on their ability to write by being asked to write extended essays. Fair enough. But unless and until students have been taught, and been given multiple opportunities to practise, each of the steps involved in essay writing, you’re unlikely to learn much about what they can actually do.
But, what is far more likely is that the children who can write with fluency are able to do so despite the fact you haven’t taught them.
No more than one new essay sentence and two new creative sentences in any half term. Everything taught earlier in the sequence is kept alive through regular retrieval practice.

The checkpoint assesses students’ ability to write what they’ve been explicitly taught: thesis statements and past participle starts. The aim is for every single child to pass the checkpoint and, if any struggle, the assumption is either there’s a problem with how the resources have been embedded into your curriculum (insufficient practice) or with how the curriculum is being taught (faulty instruction). This can then be addressed without students feeling like failures.

As we all know, assessment drives what gets taught. If Key Stage 3 assessments are extended essays marked against GCSE-style criteria, sentence work is squeezed out. But if these are replaced with short mastery assessments which assess only what has been taught, teachers will be able to find out how effective their instruction has been.
This is the hardest part for colleagues to accept. Crucially, it doesn’t mean students write less but that they write in regular, short, controlled bursts.
Probably the most important piece of advice is not to launch all three years’ content at once.
